title: Rome denies standing the strict tribunal by inherent works
source_text: XLVI. Caeterum, ut supra satis probatum est, non sentiunt homines per justitiam sibi inhaerentem, & bona sua opera, posse coram severo tribunali Dei consistere, & damnationem vitare, ac vitam aeternam consequi, si Deus ipsos, & eorum opera, rigide excutiat, nec quicquam ipsis misericorditer condonet, atque indulgeat. Itaque facile concedunt neminem eo sensu coram Deo justum reperiri, sed omnes egere divina cle-mentia, & delictorum suorum venia & remissione. Quin ultro fatentur remissionem illam, esse donum Dei plane gratuitum, quod nullis hominum meritis ex justitia de-betur: licet ipsa naturae divinae bonitas & aequitas quodammodo postulet, ut in gra-tiam recipiat eos, qui per fidem & poenitentiam, ad misericordiam ipsius confugiunt. Quo respiciunt nonnulli Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, ut Bellarminus & Becanus, dum dicunt fidem & poenitentiam mereri de congruo remissionem peccatorum. Quem tamen loquendi modum alii repudiant, ut Thomas Stapletonus.
pass_a_gloss: But, as has been sufficiently proved above, they do not think that men by the righteousness inherent in them and by their good works can stand before God's severe tribunal and avoid damnation and obtain eternal life, if God rigidly shakes them and their works and mercifully pardons and indulges them nothing. Therefore they easily concede that no one is found just before God in that sense, but that all need divine clemency and the pardon and remission of their faults. Nay, they freely confess that that remission is God's plainly free gift, which is due to no merits of men of justice: although the very goodness and equity of the divine nature in a way demands that he receive into grace those who by faith and repentance flee to his mercy. To which some doctors of the Roman Church look, as Bellarmine and Becanus, when they say that faith and repentance merit the remission of sins by congruity—which manner of speaking others, as Thomas Stapleton, reject.
pass_b_english: Rome does not claim inherent justice stands the severe tribunal without mercy.
Remission is free; some say faith/penance merit it de congruo—Stapleton and others refuse that phrase.

choices.why: Key lemma for De Justitia densify §1080.
